why: Ethiopia was occupied and annexed by Italy (Addis Ababa fell 5 May 1936) as part of Italian East Africa until the British-Ethiopian reconquest of 1941; map shows Italy in only part of the country

Tigray and Amhara were the core of the Solomonic Ethiopian Empire before the Adal invasion; map flickers every decade between the Empire and 'East African peoples' / 'Funj Sultanate' / 'Nuba and Kordofan' peoples

After the defeat of Ahmad Gragn (1543) the highlands of Tigray and Amhara (Gondar, Lasta, Begemder) stayed under the Ethiopian Empire through the Gondarine period, Zemene Mesafint and Yohannes IV; map alternates decade by decade with peoples, Funj Sultanate and 'Bedouin tribes'
Menelik II had subdued Arsi (1886), Harar (Jan 1887), Gurage (1889) and founded Addis Ababa (1886) before becoming emperor in 1889; map shows these as 'East African peoples' (a pseudo-polity) in 1890

By 1900 Menelik had conquered Wolayta, Kaffa, the Ogaden (from 1891), Borana (1896-97) and Benishangul (1898); map shows parts as Kenya [UK] and Sudan [UK] in 1900 and as 'East African peoples' in 1890
Ottomans took Massawa in 1557 and held it as Habesh Eyalet until it was transferred to Egypt in 1866; map shows Habesh only every other decade, alternating with Ethiopian Empire / Funj Sultanate
Massawa coast incorporated into Khedivial Egypt in 1866 until the Italian landing of 1885
Italy occupied Massawa in February 1885, before the 1890 proclamation of the Eritrea colony

Highland Eritrea (Hamasien, Seraye) was Medri Bahri, governed by the Bahr Negash under the Ethiopian emperor; map alternates every decade between Medri Bahri, Ethiopian Empire and 'Saharan nomads (Tuareg, Moors, Tubu)'

Medri Bahri (Bahr Negash, later the autonomous Hab Sellus rulers of Hamasien) persisted until Yohannes IV placed it under Ras Alula; map alternates every decade between Medri Bahri, Ethiopian Empire and peoples
Highlands governed directly for Yohannes IV by Ras Alula until Italian occupation (Asmara 1889, colony 1890)

After Adal's collapse the Imamate of Aussa (1577) ruled eastern Ethiopia and north-western Djibouti; map alternates every decade between Aussa and 'Ethiopian Empire 67% / Ottoman Empire 33%', neither of which held Djibouti
Tadjoura was the seat of the Afar Dardar sultans (list from 1620) until the French protectorate treaties of 1883-87; map alternates with 'Ethiopian Empire' every other decade
Obock coast belonged to the Afar sultans of Raheita until French occupation; map alternates with 'Ethiopian Empire' and 'Ottoman Empire', neither of which held it
Southern Djibouti hinterland under Afar sultanates; map alternates with 'Ethiopian Empire', which never ruled here
Gobaad sultanate in the Dikhil plain (treaty partner of France); map alternates with 'Ottoman Empire'
French Obock territory (bought 1862) was occupied and extended to Tadjoura by protectorate treaties from 1884
The Imamate of Aussa ruled the Afar lowlands of eastern Ethiopia/Djibouti, not Somaliland (only a brief seizure of Zeila 1584-89); map shows Aussa over 100% of Somaliland

Somaliland declared independence in May 1991 and has administered the former British Somaliland de facto since; map shows it on only 12% and Somalia on the rest (east of Sool/Sanaag is disputed with Puntland)

Majeerteen Sultanate became an Italian protectorate by the Alula treaty of 7 Apr 1889 but kept its own rule until conquered in the Campaign of the Sultanates (1927); map shows direct Italian Somaliland from 1890 (paper claim, not occupation)
Nugaal was Majeerteen territory under the 1889 Italian protectorate until ceded to the Dervishes in 1905

By the Illig treaty (1905) Italy ceded the Nugaal valley to Mohammed Abdullah Hassan's Dervish State (HQ at Eyl 1905-09), which lasted until the 1920 British campaign; the Dervish State is absent from the map
After the fall of the Dervishes (1920) Nugaal reverted to the Majeerteen protectorate until Italian direct rule in 1927
Hobyo became an Italian protectorate (8 Feb 1889) but stayed self-ruling until annexed in the Campaign of the Sultanates (1925-27); map shows direct Italian rule from 1890

Italy held only Benadir ports (Merca, Barawa 1893); the Geledi Sultanate at Afgooye ruled the Lower Shabelle until Italy pushed inland in 1905-08 (incorporated 1911); map shows full Italian control from 1890
Italian occupation of the interior began only with the 1905-08 campaigns and the interior towns stayed contested for years; map shows Italian Somaliland across the interior from 1890
British forces took Italian Somaliland in Feb 1941 and held it under military administration until the 1950 UN trusteeship under Italy
The Majeerteen Sultanate ruled Bari continuously from the 18th century; map replaces it for 1840-59 with an 'Omani Slave Coast' (no Omani rule in the far north-east)

Lower Shabelle was ruled by the Geledi Sultanate (Afgooye), at its height under Yusuf Mahamud and Ahmed Yusuf (d. 1878); Zanzibari claims covered only port towns. Map shows an anachronistic 'Omani Slave Coast'
Mudug was Hawiye/Hiraab country, never Omani-ruled; map shows 'Omani Slave Coast' for 1840-59
Zanzibar and Pemba formed the Sultanate of Zanzibar after the 1856 split from Oman; map labels them 'People's Republic of Zanzibar', a name from the 1964 revolution
Zanzibar and Pemba were ruled by Said bin Sultan of Oman (who moved his court to Zanzibar) until the 1856 partition; map uses an invented 'Omani Slave Coast'

The mainland coast was administered by the German East Africa Company from 1888 and, after the Abushiri revolt was crushed (1889), by German imperial forces; map shows it as British-protected Zanzibar in 1890
Morogoro was never part of Zanzibar under British protection; inland German control was still being established in the 1890s

In 1890-95 the IBEA Company effectively administered only the leased coastal strip; the East Africa Protectorate was proclaimed 1 July 1895 and interior rule came later. Map shows UK rule over most of Kenya from 1890
Nkore/Ankole (founded 15th c.) was the main kingdom of south-west Uganda until the Ankole Agreement of 1901; map drops it after 1600 for Buhweju and shows Buganda there 1810-49
These western/northern lands were Bunyoro's, not Buganda's; map shows Buganda holding half of Uganda 1810-49
Tooro broke away from Bunyoro in 1830 under Olimi I, was reabsorbed in 1876 and restored in 1891; absent from the map (shown as Buganda 1810-49)
Bunyoro, not Buganda, held Mubende and the Kiryandongo-Apac area; Buganda shown there 1810-49 is wrong
Tooro was reabsorbed into Bunyoro-Kitara 1876-1891
Tooro regained independence in 1891 (under British sponsorship) before the 1900 protectorate agreements
Map splits Rwanda in 1890 between 'Rwanda' and 'Kingdom of Rwanda' (one state)
Germany established a protectorate over the Kingdom of Rwanda in 1897 by alliance with the king, who kept ruling; map shows 'Tanzania (Tanganyika)' (wrong name and implies direct rule)
Burundi was assigned to German East Africa on paper in 1890 but not effectively controlled until the 1902-03 campaign against Mwezi IV; map shows 'German Empire' from c.1900
After the Treaty of Ikiganda (1903) the Mwami ruled under German protection until Belgian occupation in June 1916; map shows 'German Empire' then 'Tanzania (Tanganyika)'
The BSAC Pioneer Column occupied only Mashonaland in 1890; Lobengula's Ndebele kingdom (Mthwakazi) ruled Matabeleland until the First Matabele War of 1893. Map shows Rhodesia over 95% in 1890
After UDI (Nov 1965) the territory was the unrecognised state of Rhodesia; map mixes 'Zimbabwe (Rhodesia)' (the colonial label) with 'Rhodesia'
Zimbabwe Rhodesia (June 1979) followed by brief return to British control (Dec 1979) before independence as Zimbabwe in April 1980
'Cakaudrove' is a Fijian chiefdom and cannot be in Zimbabwe; before Mutapa's rise this was Shona land without a recorded state
The northern plateau (Dande, Musengezi) was the heartland of the Mutapa state; map replaces it 1520-1629 with 'Cakaudrove' (a Fijian chiefdom) and uses two names (Kingdom of Mutapa / Mutapa Empire)
Mavhura accepted Portuguese vassalage in 1629; Portuguese feiras on the plateau were destroyed by Changamire Dombo in 1693
Mutapa kept its northern plateau core until its capitals moved to Chidima (Zambezi valley) in the 18th century; map uses 'Kingdom of Mutapa ~est' (different colour)
After Mutapa withdrew to Chidima the area was under Shona chieftaincies; map shows the Fijian chiefdom 'Cakaudrove'
Changamire Dombo's Rozvi state dominated the plateau from c.1683/1693 until the Nguni/Ndebele invasions of the 1830s (subdued c.1838); map shows 'Cakaudrove' (Fijian)
Shona chieftaincies raided by the Ndebele after Rozvi collapse; map shows 'Cakaudrove' (Fijian) until 1880
'Cakaudrove' is a Fijian chiefdom; southern Zambia (Tonga/Ila plateau) had no recorded state

The Bemba paramountcy (Chitimukulu) expanded under Chileshe Chepela (1810-60) and Chitapankwa (1866-87), peaking in the 1870s, until British South Africa Company rule at the end of the 1890s; the state is missing (map shows peoples, and 'Yeke' in 1860-90)

Mwata Kazembe's Lunda kingdom crossed the Luapula c.1745-60 and ruled the valley until the British burned its capital in 1899; map shows it on 3% only and puts Msiri's Yeke (based in Katanga) on the Zambian side
Lozi rule restored after the 1864 overthrow of the Kololo; map splits the kingdom between 'Barotse Kingdom', 'Barotseland' and (1890) 'Lozi'
Barotseland became a BSAC/British protectorate (resident 1897, Lawley Concession 1898) and merged into Northern Rhodesia in 1911; map shows it as Portuguese Angola in 1900
North-western Zambia stayed British (only land further west went to Angola in 1905); map shows 'Angola [under Portugal]' here in 1900
The northern (Jere) Ngoni kingdom founded c.1850 accepted British rule only in 1904; map shows a pseudo-polity 'Bantu peoples' in 1890 and British rule from 1900
Shire Highlands protectorate (1889) ratified as the British Central Africa Protectorate in May 1891, governed from Zomba; map shows 'Bantu peoples' as a polity
Likoma island (UMCA headquarters from 1884) belongs to Malawi as an exclave in Mozambican waters; map gives it to Portuguese Mozambique and later Mozambique through 2025
Likoma part of Nyasaland within the Federation
Likoma is part of Malawi (Likoma District); map shows Mozambique
Gungunhana's Gaza Empire ruled southern Mozambique until its defeat by Portugal in 1895; map shows Portuguese rule from 1890
The Niassa Company (chartered 1891) occupied the inland concession only in 1900-02 and fought Yao chiefs until 1912; map shows Portuguese rule from 1890
'Cakaudrove' is a Fijian chiefdom; replace with no state before Mutapa
Mutapa controlled the Zambezi trade routes; map shows the Fijian chiefdom 'Cakaudrove' here 1520-1629

The VOC Cape Colony (founded 1652) covered the south-western Cape (Stellenbosch, Drakenstein, Swellendam 1745) until British occupation in 1795; map shows it only every other decade (3%) and drops it in 1700, 1710, 1730
First British occupation of the Cape 1795-1803
Cape returned to the Batavian Republic under the Peace of Amiens (1803) until the British reoccupation after Blaauwberg (1806); map shows British throughout
First British annexation of the Transvaal, 12 Apr 1877 to the Pretoria Convention (3 Aug 1881); map labels it 'British Cape Colony'
Transvaal annexed as a British colony on 1 Sept 1900 (war ended 31 May 1902) until Union in 1910; map shows the independent Boer republic until 1910
The Orange Free State was annexed as the Orange River Colony in 1900 (confirmed by the Treaty of Vereeniging 1902) until Union in 1910; map shows the Boer republic until 1910
Mutapa lay between the Zambezi and the Limpopo; it never ruled south of the Limpopo, yet the map gives it 11% of South Africa
Mutapa did not reach the lower Limpopo/Gaza; map gives it Gaza province 1450-1520

Germany never occupied Ovamboland (north of the police zone 'Red Line', ruled indirectly through the kingdoms); Ondonga stayed self-governing until South African occupation in 1915. Map shows direct German rule from 1890
No colonial power challenged the Oukwanyama kingdom until 1915; King Mandume fell fighting South African forces in Feb 1917
Western Ovambo kingdoms (Ongandjera, Uukwaluudhi etc.) lay outside German-administered territory until 1915
Hendrik Witbooi's Nama resisted German rule in 1893-94; German control of Namaland dates from the 1894 settlement, not 1890

The Merina Kingdom remained sovereign until the French took Antananarivo in 1895 (protectorate 1896, colony 1897); map replaces it in 1890 with a modern 'Madagascar (Malagasy)' covering the whole island
The south and west were never Merina-ruled; the Bara stayed independent until French conquest after 1895
The Antandroy south stayed independent of Merina rule until French conquest
Map splits the same state into 'Merina Kingdom' and 'Kingdom of Imerina ~est' (two colours)
'Cakaudrove' is a Fijian chiefdom; 'French India' (1690s) also never held this coast. No state before Ratsimilaho's Betsimisaraka confederation (1712)
Ratsimilaho's Betsimisaraka confederation (from 1712) held the north-east coast until Radama I took Toamasina in 1817; map shows the Fijian 'Cakaudrove' 1820-29
Merina conquest of the Betsimisaraka coast in 1817
'Cakaudrove' (Fiji) and, from 1620, the highland Merina Kingdom are shown in the north-west before the Sakalava Boina kingdom; Merina expansion here began only under Radama I
Imerina was a small highland state until Andrianampoinimerina reunified it from 1787; the Betsileo south of it were conquered only around 1800-1820. Map gives the Betsileo lands to Merina from 1620
South-east coast (Antambahoaka/Antemoro) was outside Merina rule until Radama I's campaigns; map gives it to Merina from 1620
Anosy was Antanosy country, not Merina (map shows Merina from 1620)
French colony of Fort-Dauphin (1643, ended by the 1674 massacre); map labels it 'New France', the name of French Canada
After the French left, Anosy returned to Antanosy rule until the Merina expansion; map shows Merina 1620-1800
Anjouan remained an independent sultanate until the 1886 French protectorate treaty (France held only Mayotte from 1841); map shows 'French India [under Kingdom of France]' from 1680
Mohéli was a local sultanate until the 1886 protectorate; map shows 'French India' from 1680
Protectorate treaties of 1886; the islands joined the colony of Madagascar in 1908
French protectorate from 1886 until incorporation into Madagascar colony in 1908; map shows 'Mozambique [under Portugal]' in 1890-1910
Permanent French settlement on Rodrigues from 1735 (subordinate to the French Mascarenes) until British capture in 1809; map shows no polity on Rodrigues ever
Rodrigues (taken 1809) and Agaléga were British dependencies of Mauritius; map shows them with no polity through 2025
Rodrigues and Agaléga are part of the Republic of Mauritius (Rodrigues autonomous since 2002); map shows no polity
French claim (1756) and settlement from 1770, administered from Isle de France, until Britain took possession in 1811; map shows the islands as empty, 'Madagascar' or 'Merina Kingdom'

British colony (dependency of Mauritius until 1903) from 1811; outer islands Aldabra, Farquhar and Des Roches were in BIOT 1965-76. Map shows most of the islands with no polity and parts under 'Merina Kingdom', 'Madagascar' and 'Comoros'
Independent republic since 29 June 1976; map shows 75% 'no polity' plus 'Comoros' and 'Madagascar' through 2025

Map shows a 'Mirambo Unyanyembe Ukimbu' state over western Tanzania in the 1890s, but Mirambo died in 1884, his Urambo alliance was confined to northern Unyamwezi (Tabora region) and never reached Kigoma, Katavi, Rukwa or Mbeya

Ngwane III (succeeded 1744) founded the Swazi (Ngwane) kingdom with its capital at Shiselweni; map shows only 'Khoisan' / 'Bantu-speaking peoples' until 1820 (Bantu-speaking farmers had been there since at least the 11th century)
Map switches to 'Kingdom of Eswatini ~est' for one decade, between 'Swazi Kingdom' before and after (same state)
